paras: The killing of Sid Dixon was the fatal shooting of a Black mill hand by armed white pursuers in western Fulton County, Kentucky, near Hickman, in October 1882. After a week of quarrels, whites calling themselves a sheriff's posse hunted Dixon and other Black men; one report said Dixon was shot dead and two others wounded, while the local paper reported only wounds.

According to The Hickman Courier, the trouble began on Friday, October 6, when Sid Dixon forced his way onto a wagon belonging to Jas. Bushart that fifteen-year-old Andrew Shaw was driving home from Hickman. The Courier said Dixon, drinking, struck a white man named Lee with a whisky jug, until John Edwards knocked him down twice with a stick. The Courier added that on Monday Dixon and two other men attacked Edwards with a slab at Linder's mill, where Dixon worked, saying the colored men "were going to stand together against the whites."

A Louisville dispatch of October 14, based on one of the hunted men, said instead that Edwards "beat him terribly" on Friday, and on Monday rode off for his gun, saying he would kill Dixon "and all his gang," so the six mill hands hid in the woods.

The Courier reported that on Monday Dixon and four other armed men fired on unarmed whites at Mc. Bushart's farm, wounding a mule. A Hickman wire dated October 10 instead said the Bushart brothers had been ambushed on the road and Mack Bushart "seriously" wounded. The whites then obtained warrants against Sid Dixon, Nick Dixon and Joe Norvell, armed themselves, enlisted officers Johnson and McMahan, and "constituted themselves a Sheriff's posse"; the wire put the sheriff's party at thirty armed men.

That evening, by the Courier's account, part of the posse came on three armed Black men at Jack Upshaw's farm, ordered them to halt, and fired when they ran; two fell but got up and escaped, leaving their guns behind. The Louisville dispatch said Edwards returned with "fourteen white ruffians" and pursued the six men until Wednesday night, when the whites ordered them to halt and fired as they obeyed, wounding two. As the men scattered, Dixon was hit between the shoulders while leaping a fence and fell dead; a wounded man named Norvill was later seen making for the state line.

On Wednesday night constable McMahan's posse captured Lewis Wisdom, a Black preacher, at Lewis Bell's house on the Troy road. Wisdom admitted firing once at the whites but said the men had armed themselves and set out for Hickman for protection because they understood the whites were hunting them to kill them. After an examining trial before Judge Murrell he was jailed to await the circuit court, and the Courier warned he might be taken out and lynched; no later report of his fate, or of an inquest into Dixon's death, appears in the coverage.

The first wire from Hickman, printed by the Washington Evening Critic on October 11, described "a band of negro desperadoes" fortifying themselves and defying the authorities, though the Critic headed it "Just Like White Kentuckians." The Hickman Courier, the local paper, told the story from the white participants' side as a "Scrimmage between Whites and Blacks" and treated the armed whites as a lawful posse, reporting no death.

The Louisville dispatch reversed the roles: the Wheeling Intelligencer headlined it "Persecuting the Black Man" and blamed the "Bourbons," and the Kennebec Journal in Maine titled its version "Kentucky's Ku Klux." Both called the hunted men "quiet and peaceable citizens," and the story ran on in New England papers through late October, including the Vermont Phoenix, the Ellsworth American and the Burrillville Gazette.

The accounts disagree on who started the violence: the Courier and the Hickman wire blamed Dixon and his armed party, while the hunted man's account blamed Edwards. They also differ on deaths, from two Black men "known to be killed" in the October 10 wire, to one in the Louisville dispatch, to none in the Courier, which placed its posse shooting on Monday evening rather than the Wednesday night the Louisville account gives.

Four papers agree that armed whites hunted and fired on Black men near Hickman (A2, A3, A5), but they disagree on who started the trouble and on deaths: the Louisville dispatch reports Dixon killed (A4, A5), the Oct. 10 wire two killed (A2), and the local Courier only two wounded (A3).

accounts.label: Hickman Courier (local white paper)
accounts.gist: Dixon provoked the quarrel and attacked Edwards; his armed squad fired on unarmed whites, who then got warrants and as a sheriff's posse fired on three fleeing men, wounding two who escaped. No death is reported.

accounts.label: Lewis Wisdom (in the Courier)
accounts.gist: He and the others armed themselves because they heard whites were hunting them to kill them, were heading to Hickman for protection, and fired when they ran on the whites.

accounts.label: One of the hunted men (Louisville dispatch)

framing.detail: The Washington Evening Critic ran the Hickman wire on 'a band of negro desperadoes' who 'defy the authorities', though under the ironic headline 'Just Like White Kentuckians.'

The Hickman Courier told the story from the whites' side as a 'Scrimmage between Whites and Blacks', blaming Dixon and treating the armed whites as a lawful sheriff's posse, while warning of a possible lynching of Wisdom.
The Morris Tribune headlined the Oct. 10 wire 'A War of Races' and 'Letting Daylight Through One Another', repeating the Busharts' version.

The Wheeling Intelligencer and Kennebec Journal ran the Louisville dispatch as 'PERSECUTING THE BLACK MAN' and 'KENTUCKY'S KU KLUX', blaming 'Bourbons' and 'white ruffians' and calling the victims 'quiet and peaceable citizens'.

conflicts.note: The Courier account comes from the white participants; the Louisville account from one of the hunted men.

The Courier is local but speaks for the white participants; the Louisville account comes from one of the hunted men.
